# Evaluation of paranasal sinuses

The crux of sinus diagnosis rests on a thorough, focused history
and physical examination. In patients who are planned to
undergo maxillary sinus floor augmentation, it is critical to elicit
a proper history and to perform a focused physical examination
on the paranasal sinuses and associated structures. Patients
who are afflicted with at least one major sinus infection every
year merit consideration of full CT evaluation. Box 2-1 summa-
rizes the most common signs and symptoms associated with
rhinosinusitis. In addition, findings such as pain with palpa-
tion or percussion over the paranasal sinuses, hearing changes,
maxillary dental pain, periorbital discomfort, sinus headache,
or turbinate hyperemia may indicate sinusitis.
CT imaging-most often CBCT-is of utmost importance in
evaluating both the maxillary edentulous ridge and the health

# References

8. Ogle OE, Weinstock RJ, Friedman E. Surgical anatomy of the
nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses. Oral Maxillofac Surg Clin
North Am 2012;24:155-166.
9. Haghnegahdar A, Khojastepour L, Naderi A. Evaluation of
FIG 10-33  Healthy maxillary sinuses.

hysiologic changes that occur in the maxilla following
the loss of teeth often do not allow for the placement of
dental implants in the posterior maxilla. Loss of alveolar
height due to periodontal disease and tooth extractions
combined with the possibility of secondary sinus pneumatization 
limit the available bone height for implant placement.
Maxillary sinus augmentation has evolved as a predictable
solution to correct this deficiency. It has been part of the authors'
surgical armamentarium for more than 30 years1 and has under-
gone many changes in surgical protocol over this time as a result
f ongoing clinical and scientific research, the development of
new products and technologies, the desire for higher proce-
ural success rates and reduced complication rates, and the
demand for minimally invasive surgical approaches. There have
been numerous transcrestal sinus elevation techniques devel-
oped that have proven to be the equal to the lateral window
approach in outcome; however, when less than 4 mm of resid-
ual crestal bone is available, the lateral window remains the
procedure of choice.
This chapter will begin with a discussion of indications and
contraindications, followed by basic sinus anatomy. Preopera-
tive treatment planning will be presented in a manner that will
provide the clinician with a means of determining whether an
interdisciplinary consultation with an ear, nose, and throat (ENT)
physician is indicated and to determine the difficulty level of
the case in question.

# ORG Linqual Brackets

ORG lingual brackets incorporate all the advantages of other cur-

.
ORG brackets are smaller than Ormco Generation 7 brackets

Hooks of one-piece construction on all brackets enable better liga-

The authors have found that most small lingual brackets lack the
option to combine elastic modules and/or power chains, and/or
metal ligatures, and/or Class II elastics. The smaller the bracket, the
greater are the chances that the elastic module will come out, which
forces clinicians to use time-consuming metal ligatures. The ORG's
hooks ensure that the elastic module will not come out. The hooks
have been declined more than 15 degrees gingivally; the hooks on
the central and lateral incisor brackets are of the ball-type design, and
the hooks on the canine brackets are of the cylinder design.

occlusal contact interference, and fewer speech problems.

xperience shows that the principal mechanical problems encoun-

slot in the posterior brackets and tubes, which facilitates torque
control and sliding mechanics, and a maximum archwire size of
0.018 × 0.025 inches (Fig 5-1).

welding. They are smooth and rounded to avoid tongue irritation
and patient discomfort (Figs 5-2 to 5-4).

widgetData.source_sentence: What type of implant is recommended for a narrow-diameter implant case according to the Esthetic Risk Assessment?
sentences:
# Treatment guidelines

Esthetic outcomes can be achieved at post-extraction
sites irrespective of the timing of implant placement.
Different placement times, however, present with spe-
cific treatment challenges and variable predictability of
esthetic outcomes.
With immediate placement, a high level of clinical com-
petence and experience in performing the treatment is
needed. Careful case selection is required to achieve sat-
isfactory esthetic outcomes. The following clinical condi-
tions should be satisfied:

# 8.1.5
Esthetic Failure Due to
Implants and Third-party
Implant Components Lacking
Scientific Validation

Clinicians are cautioned to purchase implants from
manufacturers who follow good manufacturing prac-
tices in keeping with International Organization for
Standardization (ISO) or US Food and Drug Administration 
(FDA) standards. Defects in raw materials and in the man-
ufacturing process may certainly manifest themselves, so
clinicians should be diligent in maintaining records of
product lot numbers and patients records to ensure an
appropriate response (Figs 9a-d; Dr. V. Chappuis).

# Introductory remarks

From these three systematic reviews, a general obser-
vation was made that the available data on esthetic
outcomes were predominantly represented by case
series studies. Relatively few randomized controlled
trials (RCTs) and cohort studies were identified, and a
minority of these was judged to be at low risk of bias.
Nevertheless, the case series studies provided invaluable
information in establishing the current clinical trends in
techniques and materials related to esthetic outcomes.
Indeed, well-designed prospective case series studies of
consecutively enrolled subjects with clearly defined in-
clusion and exclusion criteria can provide important in-
formation to validate clinical procedures and materials.
The group recognized that RCTs are not always feasible
or ethical when clinical conditions that are known to in-
crease the risk of adverse esthetic outcomes are under
investigation. Implant treatment in the esthetic zone is
a challenging procedure and classified as advanced or
complex according to the SAC classification (Dawson and
coworkers 2009). Most patients present with multiple es-
thetic risk factors and often have high expectations. If
esthetic complications occur, they are usually difficult or 
impossible to manage. As a consequence, the prevention 
of esthetic complications should be a primary objective.
Therefore, a conservative treatment approach is recom-
mended to facilitate successful outcomes with high pre-
dictability and a low risk of complications.

Fig 14-10  Esthetic failure due
to too deep an implant placement.

1 Standard-diameter implant, regular connection
* If three-dimensional imaging is available with the tooth in place
1 Standard-diameter implant, regular connection
2 Narrow-diameter implant, narrow connection

# Table 1   Esthetic Risk Assessment (ERA)

At implant placement, the choice of a reduced-diameter
implant combined with a perfect prosthetically-driven
position was considered adequate to avoid a wider de-
hiscence of the implant surface, simplifying the regener-
ative procedure and increasing its predictability. The use
of a titanium-zirconium alloy implant with an active sur-
face (Straumann Roxolid SLActive; Institut Straumann
AG, Basel, Switzerland) was preferred for its higher frac-
ture resistance and faster osseointegration. On the other
hand, reports or a fracture of an anterior implant in the
correct prosthetic position are very rare. In general, re-
duced-diameter implants in the esthetic zone can often
help avoid "danger zones" and reduce the risk of esthet-
ic complications.
Implant surgery was performed under local anesthesia.
After flap elevation, the xenograft appeared well inte-
grated and presented a favorable shape (Figs 16 and
17). The implant bed was prepared following the usual
protocol, and drilling was prosthetically guided using a
surgical template (Fig 18).
One Straumann Bone Level Narrow CrossFit Roxolid im-
plant (diameter 3.3 mm, length 10 mm) with a SLActive
urface (Institut Straumann AG) was inserted (Fig 19)
and achieved adequate primary stability.

implant and sensitivity of the neighboring lateral
incisor shortly after implant placement. He sought
treatment due to an abscess around the implant.

At implant placement, the choice of a reduced-diameter
implant combined with a perfect prosthetically-driven
position was considered adequate to avoid a wider de-
hiscence of the implant surface, simplifying the regener-
ative procedure and increasing its predictability. The use
of a titanium-zirconium alloy implant with an active sur-
face (Straumann Roxolid SLActive; Institut Straumann
AG, Basel, Switzerland) was preferred for its higher frac-

hand, reports or a fracture of an anterior implant in the
correct prosthetic position are very rare. In general, re-
duced-diameter implants in the esthetic zone can often
help avoid "danger zones" and reduce the risk of esthet-
ic complications.

and achieved adequate primary stability.

interproximal bone loss, the smile line, and esthetic
expectations should be considered. In cases where
the decision is difficult to make, even after the clin-
ician has evaluated these criteria, it can also be de-
cided during the regenerative surgery. In some cas-
es, the clinician should consider whether there will
be a soft tissue defect when the extraction is per-
formed during the regenerative surgery, and then
the flap design has to be at least one tooth larger. In
cases where the extraction is performed before the
idge augmentation, a complete soft tissue healing
time of about 2 months should be allowed before
the regenerative surgery.
In this chapter, technical details of interproximal
bone and soft tissue regeneration are reviewed
through a representative case of vertical periodon-
tal regeneration in combination with ridge augmen-
tation. The 55-year-old, healthy, male patient was
treated with an immediate implant at site 12 a dec-
ade previously at another clinic. The patient experi-
enced bleeding and purulent exudate around the
implant and sensitivity of the neighboring lateral
incisor shortly after implant placement. He sought
treatment due to an abscess around the implant.
